ai.title: Pertussis (Whooping Cough)
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Pertussis is a highly contagious bacterial infection causing paroxysmal cough, especially in infants. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern and confirmatory PCR or culture; severity ranges from mild cough to life‑threatening apnea. Management combines macrolide antibiotics and supportive care.

sections.p: Pertussis is infection with Bordetella pertussis, characterised by a prolonged cough with paroxysms, inspiratory whoop, and post‑tussive vomiting. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by PCR or culture from nasopharyngeal swab.
b: Clinical case definition: cough ≥2 weeks, paroxysms, inspiratory whoop, or post‑tussive vomiting.
PCR: >90% sensitivity in first 2 weeks; culture: gold standard but low yield after 2 weeks.

t.b: Confirms Bordetella pertussis; positive result confirms diagnosis, negative early does not rule out.
Definitive identification; positive after 2‑3 weeks confirms infection.
Detects recent infection; useful after 3 weeks when PCR may be negative.

sections.p: Severity is staged by cough duration and complications, especially in infants <6 months.
b: Mild: cough <2 weeks, no apnea, feeding well.
Moderate: cough 2‑4 weeks, occasional apnea, mild desaturation.
Severe: cough >4 weeks, frequent apnea, hypoxia, weight loss, or pulmonary hypertension.

sections.p: Pertussis is caused by Bordetella pertussis; in low‑resource settings co‑infection or mimics must be considered.
b: Primary: Bordetella pertussis infection (most common).
Secondary mimics: viral bronchiolitis, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae.
Co‑factors that worsen outcome: HIV infection, malnutrition, prematurity, lack of vaccination.

sections.p: The classic course has three phases: catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent.
b: Catarrhal (1‑2 weeks): mild rhinorrhea, low‑grade fever, occasional cough.
Paroxysmal (2‑6 weeks): violent coughing fits, inspiratory whoop, post‑tussive vomiting, possible apnea in infants.
Convalescent (weeks‑months): cough persists but less severe; may be triggered by infections or irritants.

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm the pathogen and assess complications.

t.b: Detects hypoxia during cough spells; low SpO2 (<92%) signals severe disease.
Identifies pneumonia or atelectasis; may be normal in pure pertussis.
Leukocytosis with lymphocytosis (>70% lymphocytes) supports pertussis.

sections.p: Complications are most common in infants and unvaccinated children.
b: Apnea lasting >20 seconds or recurrent episodes.
Severe hypoxia requiring supplemental oxygen or ventilation.
Secondary bacterial pneumonia.
Pulmonary hypertension leading to right‑heart failure.

sections.p: Treat the organism early and support the airway and nutrition.
b: Macrolide antibiotics (azithromycin or erythromycin) to eradicate Bordetella; chosen for activity and safety in infants.
Avoid fluoroquinolones in children due to cartilage toxicity.
Supportive care: humidified air, suction of secretions, monitor oxygen saturation.
Nutritional support: small, frequent feeds; consider nasogastric feeding if vomiting interferes with intake.

sections.p: Close monitoring for at least 48 h after starting antibiotics; vaccinate contacts.
b: Repeat pulse oximetry after 24 h; ensure SpO2 ≥ 94% on room air.
Give DTaP booster to children ≥6 months and Tdap to pregnant women in third trimester.
Prophylactic macrolide for household contacts within 21 days of index case.

sections.p: Several respiratory illnesses mimic pertussis, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Viral bronchiolitis: wheeze dominant, no whoop, usually RSV.
Asthma exacerbation: reversible wheeze, triggers differ, no lymphocytosis.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae: atypical pneumonia, fever higher, cough less paroxysmal.

sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring.
b: Normal white‑cell count early in disease; lymphocytosis often appears after 2 weeks.
Negative PCR after 3 weeks does not rule out pertussis; consider serology.
Chest X‑ray may be normal despite severe apnea.

whenToSeekHelp: Inability to feed leading to dehydration
Signs of shock or severe respiratory distress

faq.q: Why is a macrolide preferred over penicillin?
faq.a: Bordetella pertussis produces beta‑lactamase; macrolides inhibit protein synthesis and are safe in infants.

faq.q: Can a child be infected after completing the DTaP series?
faq.a: Yes, immunity wanes; booster doses in later childhood and Tdap in adolescents are recommended.

faq.q: What is the significance of lymphocytosis in pertussis?
faq.a: Marked lymphocytosis (>70% lymphocytes) is a hallmark and predicts severe disease, especially in infants.

exam: What bedside findings would make you suspect pertussis in a 4‑month‑old with a cough? — Paroxysmal cough, inspiratory whoop, post‑tussive vomiting, and lymphocytosis on CBC.
How would you manage a pertussis case when PCR is unavailable? — Treat empirically with a macrolide, monitor oxygenation, and give supportive care.
Which complication distinguishes severe pertussis from a simple cough? — Frequent apnea or hypoxia requiring supplemental oxygen or ventilation.
Why is erythromycin less favored than azithromycin in infants? — Azithromycin has a better safety profile, fewer gastrointestinal side effects, and once‑daily dosing.
What maternal factor increases an infant’s risk of severe pertussis? — Maternal pertussis infection within 2‑3 weeks before delivery without maternal vaccination.
How does HIV infection alter pertussis presentation? — Higher risk of prolonged disease, more severe lymphocytosis, and increased mortality.
When would you give prophylactic antibiotics to contacts? — All household members within 21 days of symptom onset, especially if unvaccinated or immunocompromised.
What red‑flag sign would prompt immediate referral to a higher‑level facility? — Recurrent apnea >20 seconds or SpO2 < 92% despite oxygen.
